transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-12-05 16:30 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ortega (Redwood SE), Lisa Tan (CTO - Peregrine), Arjun Rao (SRE), Mei Wong (ML Eng)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand Peregrine's stack (OpenAI + some self-hosted vLLM experiments), their migration drivers (cost, latency, data control), security requirements (VPC, KMS), and to scope a pilot for Dedicated.

Topics:
- Current infra and usage patterns
- Compatibility concerns (TGI/vLLM, tokenizer differences)
- Eval parity and quality regression risk
- Latency vs cost tradeoffs (batching, quantization)
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs, data residency
- Pilot scope and next steps

Transcript body:
00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, with Diego from our solutions team. How are you all doing?
00:06 Lisa Tan: Doing good, thanks. We got about forty five minutes, so wanna dive in.
00:12 Diego Ortega: awesome, quick agenda — understand your current stack and pain, show how Dedicated maps to that, and then next steps for a pilot.
00:20 Lisa Tan: Perfect. So quick background — Peregrine's been on OpenAI for text gen and chat, heavy usage, about 1.2B tokens a month. We started experimenting with vLLM for on-prem inference for lower-cost batch jobs, and a couple of teams are using TGI for some custom models. Our main drivers are cost predictability and data residency — legal wants logs kept on our side.
00:39 Maya Chen: got it. When you say vLLM experiments, are those experiments in prod or just pockets?
00:45 Mei Wong: Mostly pockets. We have a nightly batch that runs summarization and cheaper embeddings on a single A10 node, trying to cut costs. Latency sensitive stuff still goes to OpenAI because of reliability.
00:58 Arjun Rao: we also have compliance questions — need SSO, SAML, SSO for console access, and KMS integration for key management.
01:06 Diego Ortega: all common asks — our Dedicated offering supports VPC-deployed control plane and customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, plus audit logs. We can map that out.
01:15 Lisa Tan: one thing we worry about is eval parity. Our product team runs a suite of evals against OpenAI models, and we can't have regressions when switching. How do people usually validate parity?
01:27 Diego Ortega: good question — typically we run the customer's evaluation datasets on our hosted model variants and try to match tokens/temperatures; we also provide tooling to replay prompts and compare outputs. There are differences sometimes with tokenization or model variant behaviors; we can help tune and if needed keep OpenAI as fallback during rollout.
01:44 Mei Wong: is there compatibility with TGI and vLLM? Like could we re-use the same model artifacts?
01:51 Diego Ortega: short answer: yes for many cases. Redwood supports serving common model formats and provides inference config helpers; but caveat — optimizations and quantization can change outputs slightly. For vLLM/TGI, we usually recommend running a quick eval suite to check regression risk before full migration.
02:08 Lisa Tan: for quantization, we saw some hallucination differences when we used 4-bit for some models locally — how does Redwood handle that?
02:15 Diego Ortega: we have quantization profiles that are workload-aware; Redwood Optimize recommends quantization+kernel combos. But important point — quality tradeoffs exist. We recommend an eval-first approach with a canary traffic policy and threshold-based rollback.
02:32 Arjun Rao: on throughput — our nightly batch is fine but real-time latency needs to be sub-400ms 95th for chat flows. OpenAI generally meets that, but cost per token is high. Can Dedicated match that latency?
02:45 Diego Ortega: depends on model size and GPU class; Dedicated with A100-class or H100-class pools can meet sub-400ms for smaller models or with batching and prefix caching. We can provision for latency SLOs; the trade is cost/committed capacity. We can run benchmarks with your prompt distribution to produce a realistic latency/cost curve.
03:05 Lisa Tan: what's the typical uplift for running on Dedicated vs OpenAI in terms of engineering overhead?
03:11 Maya Chen: Redwood handles the runtime concerns and provides the same API surface, so engineering changes are usually small. Diego: do you want to speak to model versioning and upkeep?
03:19 Diego Ortega: yes — model version pinning and rollouts are part of the platform; we support automated canaries, A/B, and rollback. For customer-managed private deployments there's slightly more ops alignment but we provide deployment templates and runbooks.
03:32 Mei Wong: security — we need SOC2 Type II, and we need logs routed to our Splunk with 90-day retention. Is that supported?
03:40 Maya Chen: Redwood is SOC2 and we provide audit logs; for Dedicated and Private we can forward logs to customer endpoints and accommodate retention policies — will share documentation.
03:51 Arjun Rao: about tokenization — we had some weird differences in token counts moving from OpenAI to another runtime; that affected billing estimates.
03:59 Diego Ortega: tokenizer differences do happen — we include tokenizer mapping and we can help with a tokenization pass to reconcile counts. Also we support pre-tokenized payloads if that helps alignment.
04:14 Lisa Tan: how does fallback routing work? We talked about keeping OpenAI as fallback — is that out-of-the-box?
04:20 Diego Ortega: you can set routing policies — latency-first or cost-first. We also support automatic fallback to a compatible model in another pool or region. It's configurable per route.
04:29 Mei Wong: any constraints around VPC egress, our compliance team requires no public egress for certain models — can Dedicated be fully private?
04:36 Maya Chen: yes, for Private deployments or VPC-hosted Dedicated we can limit egress and support on-prem options; will need to coordinate network topology with your infra team.
04:45 Lisa Tan: pricing — high level, what's the difference between hosted and Dedicated?
04:48 Maya Chen: hosted is usage-based with per-token pricing, Dedicated is committed capacity with fixed monthly fee plus usage for bursting; we'll send a pricing deck. For heavy sustained usage Dedicated usually reduces unit cost.
04:59 Arjun Rao: about benchmarks — can you run our eval suite or do we have to run it on your side?
05:05 Diego Ortega: we can run it either way. Best practice: you share prompt sets and expected metrics, we run a controlled benchmark on the Dedicated pool and return token-level latency, cost estimates, and output diffs. We do recommend doing it on your dataset to check parity.
05:20 Lisa Tan: ok that sounds good. How long for a pilot? We're thinking 2 weeks to validate quality and latency.
05:27 Maya Chen: typical pilot is 1–4 weeks. We'll scope a 2-week pilot with one small Dedicated pool and benchmarking run in week one and a canary traffic run in week two.
05:36 Mei Wong: any gotchas with model weights — do we need to share weights or can you pull from model hubs?
05:42 Diego Ortega: depends on licensing. If models are open weights, we can pull from registry; for proprietary weights you'll need to provide them or use Private deployment. Also for matching OpenAI capabilities we often use similar open models or fine-tuned variants — we'll discuss specifics after we see your evals.
05:58 Lisa Tan: timeline — we're aiming for an internal decision by end of January. If we run a pilot mid-December that fits.
06:04 Maya Chen: great, sounds aligned. Recap / next steps: Maya to send pricing and SOC2/KMS docs; Diego to send benchmark checklist and compatibility notes for vLLM/TGI; Arjun to send prompts and usage CSV. Then schedule pilot kickoff.
06:20 Arjun Rao: noted. Quick question — for our nightly batch that runs on-prem on vLLM, could Redwood Dedicated be used to offload that and reduce ops?
06:28 Diego Ortega: yes, dedciated can handle batch workloads with cost optimizations like batching, prefix caching, and pre-warming. There may be some config changes but overall doable.
06:40 Lisa Tan: anything else from your side?
06:43 Maya Chen: nothing major, Diego?
06:45 Diego Ortega: no, just want to say we'll try to include quantization impact examples in the checklist.
06:51 Lisa Tan: OK thanks everyone, we'll wait for the docs and then set the kickoff.
06:55 Maya Chen: thanks all.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — some speaker labels may be off; a few technical terms (vLLM/TGI/KV cache) transcribed inconsistently.

References / Shared artifacts: Pricing deck (link to be sent), SOC2 + KMS docs (link), benchmark checklist (Diego to share), sample prompt CSV (customer to share).

End of transcript.
